output.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria require demonstration of dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT). DIS requires T2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 characteristic CNS locations. DIT can be shown by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, or by new lesions on follow-up MRI, or by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands.

results.key_findings: NMOSD with AQP4-IgG positive requires at least one core clinical characteristic (optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, brainstem syndrome, diencephalic syndrome, or cerebral syndrome). AQP4-IgG negative NMOSD requires more stringent clinical and MRI criteria. Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 vertebral segments) and area postrema involvement are hallmarks.
results.title: International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders

results.key_findings: Key distinguishing features of MS vs NMOSD include: MS has periventricular Dawson fingers and short spinal cord lesions, while NMOSD has LETM and area postrema lesions. Oligoclonal bands present in >90% of MS but only ~20% of NMOSD. AQP4-IgG seropositivity is highly specific for NMOSD.
results.title: Distinguishing multiple sclerosis from AQP4-NMOSD and MOG-antibody disease

output.summary: The differentiation between MS and NMOSD requires consideration of several key imaging and laboratory features. MS typically presents with periventricular ovoid lesions (Dawson fingers), short-segment spinal cord lesions (<3 vertebral segments), and CSF oligoclonal bands (>90% of cases). NMOSD is characterized by longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 segments), area postrema involvement, and AQP4-IgG positivity. Clinical correlation with laboratory and imaging findings is required to distinguish these entities.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient (especially with high index) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with second-degree AV block, prior MI, or severe sleep apnea
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management
required_recommendations: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain and spinal-cord MRI in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)

Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by demonstrating simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (per the 2024 revised McDonald)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days), with plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe relapses
Initiate a disease-modifying therapy (DMT) after relapse stabilization; choice between platform vs. high-efficacy agent based on disease activity, MRI burden, and patient preference
Check JC virus antibody serostatus before considering natalizumab; verify up-to-date vaccinations (especially live-attenuated) before initiating B-cell depleting or S1P-modulator DMTs
Counsel on Uhthoff phenomenon, heat avoidance, smoking cessation, and vitamin D supplementation as modifiable lifestyle factors

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; ordering CT delays diagnosis and adds radiation without clinical benefit.
No cardiac indication in a typical MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not as part of MS diagnostic workup.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis or DMT decisions; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and adds substantial cost.

differential.key_features: AQP4-IgG positivity, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 vertebral segments), severe or bilateral optic neuritis, and area postrema syndrome — must be excluded before committing to MS
MOG-IgG positivity (cell-based assay), often bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis, ADEM-like presentations in younger patients, frequent lesion resolution on follow-up MRI
Leptomeningeal/pachymeningeal enhancement, hypothalamic-pituitary involvement, cranial neuropathies, hilar adenopathy on imaging, elevated serum/CSF ACE, lymphopenia
Elevated ESR/CRP, multifocal infarcts crossing vascular territories, vessel-wall enhancement on high-resolution MRA, systemic features (rash, arthritis, renal involvement)
Encephalopathy + branch retinal artery occlusion + sensorineural hearing loss; corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions characteristic
Monophasic course, post-infectious/post-vaccination trigger, encephalopathy hallmark, large confluent lesions that often resolve

key_clinical_evidence: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: the 2024 revised McDonald requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it

MS-typical MRI regions are periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord — recognising a lesion in three of these regions establishes DIS for an attack-meeting clinical event

CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands not present in paired serum) can substitute for DIT under the 2024 revised McDonald when DIS is met — this changes the calculus for clinically isolated syndromes

Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, dorsolateral or dorsal-column spinal cord lesions strongly favour MS over NMOSD (which characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)
Open-ring enhancement with the opening oriented toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of demyelination, distinguishing tumefactive MS from neoplasm and abscess
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays, not ELISA — the older ELISA-based AQP4 assays have unacceptable false-negative rates
T1 hypointense 'black holes' indicate axonal loss from prior inflammatory episodes and contribute evidence of dissemination in time even without simultaneous enhancing lesions

Choice of DMT — platform agent (interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) vs. high-efficacy agent (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine, S1P modulators) — should weigh disease activity, MRI burden, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
Low serum vitamin D is a known MS risk factor and a modifiable comorbidity; while it is NOT a diagnostic criterion, supplementation is part of comprehensive management

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Denise Carter is a 37-year-old right-handed African American woman who presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of progressive visual loss in her right eye accompanied by a deep, aching retro-orbital pain that worsens with eye movements, particularly lateral gaze and upward gaze. She initially noticed mild blurring of her right visual field while grading papers four evenings ago, which she attributed to eye strain after prolonged screen use. Over the subsequent 48 hours, the blurring progressed substantially, and she began to notice that colors, especially reds and greens, appeared faded or washed out when she covered her left eye and looked solely through the right. The retro-orbital pain developed on the second day and has been constant, rated at 5 out of 10 in intensity, worsened by eye movement but not by bright light. By the morning of presentation, she described her right eye vision as looking through a frosted window, with only vague outlines visible, which prompted her husband to bring her to the emergency department. On further questioning, she reports that approximately eight months ago she experienced a prolonged episode of numbness and tingling affecting both lower extremities from the mid-thigh downward, which developed over two to three days and persisted for roughly four weeks before gradually resolving. She visited an urgent care clinic at that time and was told it was likely a pinched nerve in her back, but no imaging studies were obtained. She notes that she still occasionally experiences brief tingling in her feet, particularly in the evenings or when she is fatigued. She also describes an unusual phenomenon in which her vision becomes noticeably worse when she takes hot showers or after vigorous exercise, though it returns to baseline after cooling down. Over the past several months, she reports progressive fatigue that is disproportionate to her activity level, difficulty concentrating during afternoon classes, and an episode approximately three months ago where her right leg felt unusually heavy and stiff while walking up stairs, which resolved after resting for several minutes. She denies any fevers, unintentional weight loss, joint pain, skin rashes, oral ulcers, dry eyes, or dry mouth. She denies any history of seizures, difficulty swallowing, or bowel or bladder incontinence, although she notes increased urinary frequency over the past two months that she had attributed to drinking more coffee.
